title: Indian Markets Hit Six-Week Low as Oil Fears and Rate Hike Worries Drag Sensex Down 353 Points
excerpt: The Sensex fell 0.46% to 76,163 with 14 of 16 sectors in the red, as Middle East tensions pushed Brent crude to $96.8 and strong U.S. jobs data reinforced Fed rate hike expectations.
body:
• Sensex closed at 76,163, down 353 points (0.46%), while Nifty ended at 23,779, down 0.5% — both at six-week lows with 14 of 16 major sectors declining.
  • Top Nifty 50 gainers: Apollo Hospitals (+1.59%), Eicher Motors (+1.05%), Maruti Suzuki (+0.94%). Top losers: Infosys (-3.80%), SBI Life (-2.42%), Tech Mahindra (-2.29%).
  • Brent crude rose to $96.8/barrel after U.S.-Iran clashes in the Strait of Hormuz escalated, stoking inflation fears.
  • Market breadth was sharply negative with a 180:319 advance-decline ratio on BSE500, reflecting broad risk-off sentiment.

A Broad-Based Selloff

Indian equities extended their losing streak on Monday, with the benchmark Sensex falling 352.77 points or 0.46% to close at 76,162.66 and the Nifty 50 dropping 0.5% to settle at 23,779.15. Both indices hit their lowest levels in six weeks as a combination of geopolitical tension and hawkish U.S. monetary policy expectations weighed on sentiment.

The selling was widespread. Only seven of 38 tracked sectors advanced, while 31 declined. Market breadth on the BSE500 was decisively negative, with just 180 stocks advancing against 319 declines — a ratio of 0.56, indicating nearly twice as many losers as gainers.

What Drove the Decline

Two global forces converged to pressure Indian markets. Brent crude futures rose 0.6% to $96.8 per barrel after U.S. and Iranian forces struck vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, the latest escalation in Middle East tensions that threatens global energy supply. Higher oil prices hit India — the world's third-largest crude importer — particularly hard, stoking inflation fears.

Simultaneously, stronger-than-expected U.S. jobs data reinforced expectations that the Federal Reserve may hike rates in September rather than hold steady. The prospect of higher U.S. rates pressured emerging-market assets broadly and hit Indian IT stocks especially hard, given their heavy revenue dependence on American clients.

"Market instability with a downward bias will continue in the short term due to periodic conflicts and higher crude oil prices."

— G. Chokkalingam, Founder, Equinomics Research

Winners and Losers

On the Nifty 50, Apollo Hospitals led the gainers with a 1.59% rise, followed by Eicher Motors (+1.05%) and Maruti Suzuki (+0.94%). Tata Consumer Products (+0.82%) and Max Healthcare (+0.67%) rounded out the green. Defensive healthcare and auto stocks attracted selective buying amid the broader risk-off mood.

The losers list was dominated by technology names. Infosys fell 3.80%, while Tech Mahindra shed 2.29%. Beyond tech, SBI Life Insurance dropped 2.42%, Jio Financial Services declined 2%, and Tata Steel lost 2% as metals came under pressure from global growth concerns.

Among broader stocks, Syrma SGS Technologies surged 10.81% on the BSE500, while HEG plunged 63.93%. PVR Inox dropped 7.83% on reports of an internal investigation into alleged kickbacks, though the company denied the findings. Zee Entertainment fell 6.4% after India's premier investigating agency reportedly filed an FIR against founder Subhash Chandra.

Sectoral Picture

The Nifty IT index was the biggest sectoral loser, falling 2.3%. The Nifty Media index plunged 2.81%, the worst among all sectors, driven by the PVR Inox and Zee declines. Banking, consumer discretionary, and metal indices also logged losses.

The sole bright spot was telecom, with the S&P BSE Telecommunication index rising 1.33%. Small-caps managed a modest 0.14% gain, showing pockets of resilience, while mid-caps fell 0.42% and large-caps dropped 0.48%.

The Bigger Picture

Monday's decline extends a four-week slide that has seen the Nifty and Sensex shed 2.7% and 2.5% respectively. The Sensex now trades below both its 50-day and 200-day moving averages — a bearish technical signal. Analysts also pointed to liquidity pressures from a rush of IPOs and weaker monsoon rainfall as additional headwinds.

For diaspora investors tracking Indian markets, the near-term outlook hinges on the Fed's September decision, the trajectory of crude oil prices, and whether domestic earnings season — now weeks away — can provide a catalyst to reverse the downtrend. The continued FII outflows suggest global investors remain cautious on India at current valuations.
